## Summary

His current PR conventions, verbatim:

- **human written title** for the PR
- **one line of human written text** about what the change is
- **before/after table with screenshots**
- if relevant, **a link to a clickable prototype**, "so you don't have to pull the branch and/or get the app in to right state in a dev version to see the new ux"
- **agent written pr description in collapsible `<details>` tag**

The screenshot proves the convention live: PR "Update modal that shows after making a new folder to link to new connectors" (+252 −65) carries the human comment ("replace the new folder wizard's 'soon' rows with crm, agent and tool rows that link to where you connect them" + "see prototype here:"), a Before/After pair of UI screenshots (placeholder "SOON" rows → real Connect-your-CRM / agents / tools rows), and a "Generated by Claude" description section.

## Why it matters

- The division of labor is the idea: **humans own the why-and-what (title, one-liner, before/after, prototype pointer); the agent's verbose output is demoted to a collapsed appendix.** Reviewer attention goes to intent and visible delta, not generated prose — and the prototype link kills the "pull the branch and get the app running" tax for UX changes.
- Direct upgrade to the standing deltaviz-lite experiment (Inbox, 2026-11-09): same genre — PR presentation as reviewer ergonomics — but this adds the two strongest pieces, before/after screenshots and the `<details>` demotion of agent text. Natural to trial together on our own repos (wa-bridge.mjs, desk dashboards), where every git change already goes through PR + AI review.
- Skepticism gates: light — workflow craft, not claims. Two caveats: before/after screenshot tables rot when the UI moves (they must be cheap to regenerate), and a clickable prototype needs preview-infra the desk dashboards don't have — static screenshots are our realistic version.
